title: Lower-Leaf Yellowing
summary: Yellowing that begins on older or lower leaves is a location pattern, not a diagnosis. It can reflect normal senescence, mobile-nutrient limitations, root stress, irrigation problems, salinity, or reduced light exposure.
patternQuestions: Does yellowing begin uniformly or between veins?
Is it limited to heavily shaded lower leaves or progressing upward?
Are roots healthy and actively growing?
Did irrigation, feed strength, pH, or environmental demand change recently?
possibleCategories: Systemic disease or other whole-plant stress
discriminatingChecks: Measure pH and EC using a consistent method
Compare shaded and well-lit lower leaves
Track whether new symptoms continue after root-zone conditions are corrected
redFlags: Root sloughing or loss of fine roots

title: New-Growth Chlorosis
summary: Pale or yellow new growth can result from root-zone chemistry, micronutrient availability, rapid growth, root injury, pests, pathogens, or genetic/developmental variation.
patternQuestions: Are veins greener than the tissue between them?
Is the newest tissue distorted as well as pale?
Is the symptom present on every branch or only selected growing tips?
Are roots and pH conditions normal for the system?
discriminatingChecks: Use laboratory testing when systemic infection remains plausible
redFlags: Multiple plants linked to the same propagation source

title: Interveinal Chlorosis
summary: Interveinal chlorosis means tissue between veins becomes paler while veins remain comparatively greener. The leaf age where it begins and the root-zone context are critical evidence.
patternQuestions: Does it begin on older, middle, or newest leaves?
Are the veins truly greener or is the whole leaf fading?
Is necrosis developing between veins?
Is the pattern symmetric across the leaf?
discriminatingChecks: Map symptom onset by leaf age
Review feed composition and recent changes
Compare with unaffected plants under the same environment

title: Marginal Necrosis / Leaf-Edge Burn
summary: Browning or death along leaf margins can arise from salinity, water stress, nutrient imbalance, heat or desiccation, root problems, or disease. Margin injury should be mapped by leaf age and canopy location.
patternQuestions: Does injury begin at tips and move along margins?
Are upper leaves more affected than lower leaves?
Is the root zone unusually dry, wet, saline, hot, or cold?
Did the injury appear suddenly after a feed, spray, or weather event?
discriminatingChecks: Map injury against light and airflow zones
Review recent sprays and irrigation events
redFlags: Sudden widespread injury after one event
Stem lesions or one-sided branch decline

title: Leaf Tip Burn
summary: Necrosis at leaf tips is common but nonspecific. It may appear with high root-zone ionic concentration, water-balance stress, nutrient imbalance, or prior injury.
patternQuestions: Is only the terminal tip affected or are margins progressing too?
Are many leaves affected at the same time?
Is EC elevated relative to the crop's recent baseline?
Are leaf posture and transpiration conditions otherwise normal?
discriminatingChecks: Measure root-zone EC with a documented method

title: Necrotic Spots & Lesions
summary: Dead spots can come from pathogens, pests, droplets, sprays, nutrient-related tissue failure, physical injury, or environmental damage. Lesion shape alone is rarely enough to identify cause.
patternQuestions: Are spots bounded by veins or randomly distributed?
Do lesions expand over time?
Are there halos, concentric zones, fungal growth, frass, or insects?
Do spots align with spray droplets or wetting patterns?
discriminatingChecks: Compare upper and lower leaf surfaces
Submit samples for laboratory diagnosis when disease is plausible and consequential
redFlags: Similar lesions spreading between nearby plants

title: Upward Curl / Tacoing
summary: Leaf margins curling upward can be associated with high radiant load, heat, low humidity, airflow, root-water limitations, genetics, or other stress. It should be interpreted alongside leaf temperature and canopy position.
patternQuestions: Is the symptom concentrated near the light or hottest canopy zone?
Are leaf temperatures elevated relative to air?
Does curl improve during lower-demand periods?
Are roots and substrate moisture adequate?
redFlags: Symptoms continuing after environmental demand is reduced

title: Downward Clawing
summary: Downward-curled leaflet tips can accompany excess nitrogen availability, root-zone stress, chronic saturation, salinity, genetics, or other physiological stress. Shape alone does not establish nutrient excess.
patternQuestions: Are leaves unusually dark and glossy or simply curled?
Is media persistently wet?
Is EC elevated?
Are roots healthy?
Does the pattern begin on new or older foliage?
discriminatingChecks: Track posture on new leaves after conditions change

title: Wilting
summary: Wilting indicates insufficient tissue turgor but can occur when the root zone is too dry, too wet, oxygen-limited, damaged, saline, hot, cold, or unable to meet atmospheric demand.
patternQuestions: Is the substrate dry, saturated, or apparently normal?
Does the plant recover during lower-demand periods?
Are roots intact?
Is wilting whole-plant or limited to one branch?
discriminatingChecks: Compare leaf temperature and VPD context
Inspect stem injury when only one branch wilts

title: Bleaching & High-Light Injury
summary: Very pale or bleached upper-canopy tissue can result from excessive light/radiant exposure, heat, chemical injury, or other stress. Location relative to the light source is important evidence.
patternQuestions: Is bleaching strongest at the highest or most exposed sites?
What are PPFD and leaf temperature at those points?
Is there a sharp exposure boundary?
Did fixture height, power, or environment change recently?
discriminatingChecks: Inspect for residue or spray history

title: Purple or Red Pigmentation
summary: Anthocyanin-related purple or red coloration can be genetic or developmentally normal, and can also increase with temperature, nutrient, root, or other stress. Pigment color alone is not a deficiency diagnosis.
patternQuestions: Is the cultivar known for pigmentation?
Are leaves otherwise healthy and growing normally?
Did cool temperatures precede the change?
Are petioles, stems, veins, or whole leaves affected?
discriminatingChecks: Check whether other stress symptoms are present

title: Stalled or Slow Growth
summary: Slow growth is an outcome shared by many root, environmental, nutritional, pest, pathogen, genetic, and developmental conditions. Growth rate should be compared with stage and recent baseline.
patternQuestions: Did growth slow suddenly or has the plant always been slower?
Are roots expanding?
Are temperature, light, and water conditions suitable?
Is the issue one plant, one cultivar, or the whole crop?
discriminatingChecks: Use magnification and testing where biological agents are plausible
redFlags: Progressive loss of vigor across clones

title: Distorted New Growth
summary: Twisted, hardened, blistered, narrowed, or malformed new leaves can arise from microscopic mites, chemical injury, root-zone problems, micronutrient availability, systemic pathogens, or developmental abnormalities.
patternQuestions: Are the newest tissues most affected?
Is bronzing or russeting present?
Were sprays or chemicals recently applied?
Are multiple clones from one source affected?
discriminatingChecks: Use high magnification on growing tips
Test for systemic pathogens when epidemiology supports it

title: Root Discoloration & Sloughing
summary: Root color varies with age, substrate, and staining. Loss of fine roots, soft texture, sloughing, poor branching, and declining function are more informative than color alone.
patternQuestions: Are roots firm or soft?
Are fine white or light-colored root tips still forming?
Is the media persistently saturated?
Are there odors, biofilms, heat, or high EC?
discriminatingChecks: Measure moisture, EC, pH, and root-zone temperature
Use laboratory diagnosis when pathogen identity matters
redFlags: Multiple plants linked through shared water

title: Stem Lesions & Branch-Specific Decline
summary: Localized stem damage can interrupt support or transport and may result from physical injury, pathogens, constriction, insects, or training wounds. Branch-specific symptoms should trigger direct stem inspection.
patternQuestions: Is decline limited above one stem location?
Is there splitting, constriction, discoloration, soft tissue, or callus?
Was the branch recently trained or tied?
Are insects, frass, or fungal structures present?
discriminatingChecks: Inspect the entire stem below affected foliage
Submit samples when a stem pathogen is plausible
redFlags: Multiple plants with similar stem lesions

title: Flower Browning, Collapse & Rot
summary: Browning inside or around flowers can reflect Botrytis and other molds, senescent tissue, mechanical damage, insect injury, heat, or desiccation. Dense flowers must be opened and inspected internally when rot is suspected.
patternQuestions: Does browning begin inside dense flower tissue?
Is gray or other fungal growth present?
Did rain, condensation, or high humidity occur?
Are dead leaves embedded in the flower?
